target_customer: Academic, biotech and pharma labs that buy low-cost pipetting and lab automation robots, plus OEM partners
problem: Liquid handling robots cost 10,000 to 25,000 dollars or more and were closed to customization, leaving many biologists pipetting by hand.
business_model: Hardware sales (robots, pipettes, modules, consumables) plus software and services

founders.name: Nicholas Wagner
founders.background_notes: Per YC page. Co-built the first prototype with Chau (SynBioBeta, Oct 2014).

founders.name: Will Canine
founders.background_notes: Co-founder and interviewee in SynBioBeta 2014 piece.

founders.name: Chiu Chau
founders.background_notes: SynBioBeta (Oct 2014) says he worked with lab automation equipment for over fifteen years and built the first prototype.

technical_complexity.rationale: Mechatronics, firmware and a Python API for a precise pipetting robot at low cost; standard hardware engineering with calibration and reliability challenges.

defensibility.rationale: Open software and a user community and protocol library create stickiness, but the hardware itself was copyable and later became proprietary.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Large incumbents did not match the 2,000 to 4,000 dollar price point in the sources opened; no acquisition found.

market_need_then: SynBioBeta (Oct 2014) cited existing pipetting robots at about 15,000 dollars and 3-axis robots from about 25,000 dollars or budget options near 10,000, closed to innovation; Kickstarter raised 126,000 dollars from 237 backers per a search summary.

branding.domain_note: Uses opentrons.com; no acquisition story found.

identity.logo: Drop shaped mark per trademark notice (Opentrons drop logo)
identity.voice_and_tone: Tagline Automation without the gatekeeping and We make robots for biologists

branding.community_and_virality: Started in the DIYbio community at Genspace in Brooklyn and via a Kickstarter; Wikipedia credits OT-1 as first commercial open-source liquid handling robot.

brand_strength.rationale: Open-source identity, DIYbio roots and published protocols and citations made it a recognized name in lab automation, which helped drive adoption.

pivots.from: OT-One open hardware robot for hackers
pivots.to: Proprietary OT-2 for mainstream labs and later Flex
pivots.why: Move from hobbyist to lab market; hardware became proprietary per Wikipedia

outcome_analysis: Opentrons began as a DIYbio Kickstarter robot in 2014, joined YC in Winter 2016, raised a 10 million dollar seed in 2018 alongside the 4,000 dollar OT-2, then a 200 million dollar Series C in 2021 and later rounds. It stays active, selling a lower-cost alternative to incumbent robots and adding AI tools, with no shutdown found.
notes: Fierce Biotech returned 403, not worked around. 2018 seed is from VentureBeat and Fierce/SiliconANGLE headlines in search results. Series B around August 2020 of about 21 million dollars appears only in aggregator listings (startupintros, seedtable) so it is unverified and not recorded as a round. Pre-YC seed (2014 to 2016, a 7 million dollar seed in March 2016 or 7.2 million in 2017 per aggregators) is unverified. Series E 40 million is reported by Pulse2 and CityBiz with Avego lead; exact date unclear (late Oct 2026), so year only; stage recorded as series_d_plus because a Series D was not found. CB Insights lists a Series C II of 20 million in Dec 2025 (aggregator, unverified). Competitors: only unnamed incumbents in dated sources; Tecan, Hudson, Sartorius named in an undated Labcritics page, so not listed. Outcome search found no layoffs, lawsuit or acquisition. Founder Wagner's current work per YC page is quant research feeding generative AI.
